kind: multi_country_combination
status: approved
buttonLabel: "Learn more about routes through Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Peru"
lead: >-
  Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Peru offer a chance to see Iguazu Falls, high-altitude Andean lagoons, the Uyuni Salt Flat, Lake Titicaca and Machu Picchu in a single journey. In the Ada Tours catalogue, the selected four countries are part of the main routes, but the current itineraries also visit Chile. The journey into Bolivia runs via Santiago and the Atacama Desert. The key considerations are the length of the mountain section, border crossings, Machu Picchu reservations and document requirements in all five countries.
---

## Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Peru: what connects these countries

**The most substantial part of this journey runs from the Bolivian plateau to the Peruvian Andes.** Before reaching it, travellers have time to see [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/), both sides of [Iguazu Falls](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/) and [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/). The route then continues through Chile, the Uyuni Salt Flat, [La Paz](/bolivia/place/la-paz/), [Lake Titicaca](/peru/place/puno-and-lake-titicaca/), [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/) and [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/).

Our selection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. However, **every current tour actually covers five countries**: in addition to Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Peru, it visits [Chile](/chile/). The journey into Bolivia passes through [Santiago de Chile](/chile/place/santiago-de-chile/) and [San Pedro de Atacama](/chile/place/san-pedro-de-atacama/). It is important to understand this geography from the outset rather than expect a four-country itinerary without Chilean flights or a border crossing.

| Journey section | What matters |
|---|---|
| Rio and Iguazu | Borders and airports |
| Chile → Bolivia | Altitude and 4×4 vehicles |
| La Paz → Puno | Titicaca and the border |
| Cusco | Machu Picchu tickets |

Unlike the usual [Peru tour catalogue](/peru/tour/), this selection lets you compare trips in which Peru's sights form the finale of a much longer journey. The number of days available in each country is affected by flights and overland transfers earlier in the itinerary.

## Why the Peruvian section cannot be left to whatever time remains

In the confirmed itineraries, Peru comes after Bolivia. Travellers travel via [Puno and Lake Titicaca](/peru/place/puno-and-lake-titicaca/) to [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/), then visit [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/) and finish in [Lima](/peru/place/lima/). This involves several separate logistical considerations: crossing the border, travelling between cities, reaching the archaeological site, arriving at the designated entry time and catching the onward flight.

**Entry to Machu Picchu is tied to a particular ticket, date, time and visitor circuit.** Peru's Ministry of Culture operates the official ticketing system and regulates access. Machu Picchu cannot simply be treated as a "free day in Cusco" with arrangements left until arrival. Train or other agreed transport schedules must align with the entry slot. When comparing Ada Tours itineraries, check which tickets and transfers are included in the specific offer.

[Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/) is a mountain city where visitors need to pay attention to how they feel. Even spending several days in Bolivia beforehand does not guarantee acclimatisation. The route from [La Paz](/bolivia/place/la-paz/) via Titicaca to Cusco is best considered in terms of overnight elevations, rather than just time spent in a vehicle.

Finally, [Lima](/peru/place/lima/), at the end of the itinerary, lies on the Pacific coast, with very different weather and altitude from Cusco. Check the final domestic flight alongside your international flight home. If the tickets are booked separately, a disruption to the domestic service could cause you to miss the onward connection.

## The Bolivia–Peru border: what happens between La Paz and Puno

[La Paz](/bolivia/place/la-paz/) and [Puno](/peru/place/puno-and-lake-titicaca/) look close together on a map of the Andes, but they are separated by an international border. Travellers must account for their right to enter Peru, the required documents and time at border control. Any subsequent excursions on Titicaca need to allow for arrival by road rather than rely on the straight-line distance between the cities.

Lake Titicaca is also a high-altitude destination. The CDC identifies the Titicaca, La Paz and Cusco areas as places where altitude sickness may occur. Travelling by bus rather than climbing a mountain does not make exposure to altitude automatically safe. Visitors from lowland cities and travellers with chronic conditions should discuss the journey individually with a doctor and check their insurance.

If the itinerary includes the Uros Islands, check which day the visit takes place and how much time remains before the next transfer. Weather on the lake may affect boat excursions. A meaningful visit to the Titicaca area needs sufficient time; an excessively tight connection reduces the stop to a brief transit.

## Iguazu at the start of the journey: do not confuse the two airports

The Brazil-to-Argentina section passes through two well-known towns: [Foz do Iguacu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/) and [Puerto Iguazu](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/). Seeing the waterfalls from both countries requires different national-park routes and an actual border crossing. In a busy itinerary, this takes up a significant part of the day.

Airport codes are crucial: **IGU** is Foz do Iguacu in Brazil, while **IGR** is Puerto Iguazu in Argentina. Later, when arriving in [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/), check whether the airport is **EZE** or **AEP**. An overland transfer is needed between the two if the following flight departs from the other airport.

On a five-country itinerary, one missed flight early in the journey could disrupt tickets booked for later stages, including visits in Peru. It therefore makes sense not to cut border-crossing and connection times just to fit in an extra excursion.

## Chile is an essential fifth stage, not an optional excursion

All four current itineraries in this catalogue include [Santiago de Chile](/chile/place/santiago-de-chile/), [San Pedro de Atacama](/chile/place/san-pedro-de-atacama/) and the onward journey into Bolivia. Chile is a substantial part of the main route. Removing it would require restructuring domestic flights and the mountain section; simply declining one excursion would not be enough.

The Atacama replaces cityscapes with dry high-altitude landscapes. Next come [Laguna Colorada](/bolivia/place/laguna-colorada/) and [Uyuni](/bolivia/place/uyuni/). Warm clothes for cold mornings, sun protection, 4×4 journeys and the length of overnight stops all matter here. Your packing needs to accommodate both tropical Brazil and the Andean plateau.

When crossing into Chile, the **SAG** service requires declarations for products of animal and plant origin. Food items in luggage must be declared correctly, and an inspector decides whether they can enter. Border documentation requirements depend on citizenship and direction of travel.

## Five currencies and documents for a long journey

The trip involves **BRL** in Brazil, **ARS** in Argentina, **CLP** in Chile, **BOB** in Bolivia and **PEN** in Peru. Plan currency exchanges around the services already included in your particular itinerary. Different payment methods can be useful for expenses in cities and remote areas. Do not assume that a single currency will be accepted throughout all five countries.

The same applies to bank cards: confirm with your issuing bank that your card will work. Visa and Mastercard cards issued in Russia do not work abroad; the availability of international cards issued by other banks depends on their issuance, fees and restrictions. Cash may be important in smaller towns in Bolivia and Peru.

For Russian citizens, the Brazilian consulate confirms short-term visa-free tourist entry for up to 90 days within a 180-day period. **This does not establish a single visa-free regime for all five countries.** Check Argentina, Chile, Bolivia and Peru separately according to your nationality, transit stops, purpose and length of stay. Peru's migration authority specifies that passports must have at least six months' remaining validity for tourist entry. Chile uses the *Permanencia Transitoria* category, under which advance visa requirements depend on the passport.

Insurance is another consideration. For overland excursions at altitude, check whether your policy covers the relevant elevation and planned activities. Medical insurance also matters for entry to Argentina under immigration rules. It is best to clarify your policy's terms before buying flight tickets.

## Choosing between four Ada Tours itineraries

The current range includes four confirmed alternatives covering the same **five countries**, but with different durations and events:

- [5 Latin American countries in 18 days](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/) — a group itinerary via Iguazu, Atacama, Uyuni, Titicaca and Machu Picchu. Useful for understanding the basic sequence of transfers.
- [Highlights of 5 countries in 19 days](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-carnival-private-tour/) — a private itinerary with a Carnival section in Rio, worth comparing with group tours for guiding languages and conditions.
- [19-day New Year itinerary](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-new-year-group-tour-19-days/) — a group tour celebrating New Year on Copacabana and continuing to Machu Picchu.
- [5 countries with the Carnival Champions' Parade in 18 days](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-rio-champions-parade-18-days/) — a group tour that includes Champions' Parade tickets and an organised transfer to the Sambadrome.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_source_5_stran_latinskoj_ameriki,tour_source_karnaval_5_stran,tour_source_5_stran_latinskoj_ameriki_na_16_dnej_na_novyj_god,tour_source_5_stran_latinskoj_ameriki_i_parad_chempionov_karnavala}}

If Machu Picchu is the priority, start by comparing the Peru days: the excursion day, included tickets and time in Cusco. If [Uyuni](/bolivia/place/uyuni/) matters more, look at the 4×4 itinerary and overnight stays. If your main reason to go is Rio Carnival, your choice is constrained by the event calendar and the confirmed conditions of each programme.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can I travel through the four countries without Chile?

This page lists current tours in which **Chile is also an essential country on the itinerary**. Excluding it would require a separate programme with a different sequence of flights and transfers. The catalogue does not confirm that a ready-made replacement exists.

### Should I book Machu Picchu admission in advance?

Yes. Plan your visit through the official ticketing system, selecting a date and entry time. Availability and visitor circuits are regulated. When booking a tour, check that the specific programme includes the necessary admission tickets and transportation.

### Which is more challenging: Uyuni or Machu Picchu?

They involve different challenges. At Uyuni, altitude, cold weather and long 4×4 drives matter; at Machu Picchu, timed entry, transport and the actual walking circuit matter. Cusco and Titicaca are also high above sea level.

### How long does the journey take?

The available itineraries last 18–19 days, including Chile. Actual time in each city depends on the number of international and domestic flights. For a longer exploration of Peru or Bolivia alone, consider the relevant single-country itineraries.

### Can I pay in US dollars throughout the journey?

US dollars are not universally accepted in all five countries. Currency exchange is possible in some places, but local currency is often more convenient for small purchases. Check which expenses are already covered by the tour and prepare a backup payment method.

Brazil and Argentina add walks beside Iguazu Falls, while Peru offers journeys through the Andes and an excursion to Machu Picchu. ## What makes this combination an adventure

**The main challenge on current itineraries is the long high-altitude journey through Bolivia.** Travellers see geothermal fields, lagoons and the Uyuni Salt Flat. Before that, they visit Rio and both sides of Iguazu; after the Bolivian stage, they continue to Titicaca, Cusco and Machu Picchu. The journey includes days with very different levels of activity: easy city tours, walks on national-park paths and remote off-road stages.

In the Ada Tours catalogue, you will find {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} that include Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Peru as principal countries. This is **a geographical intersection within a longer journey**: the itineraries also pass through Chile, and some continue through Uruguay, Ecuador or Colombia. This selection does not promise a standalone trip restricted to the four named countries. For a comparison without the adventure filter, see the [general catalogue for this combination](/multi-country/argentina_bolivia_brazil_peru/).

## Brazil and Argentina: active walks at Iguazu

After [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/), the basic itinerary goes to [Foz do Iguacu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/). On the Brazilian side, visitor paths and viewpoints provide panoramic views of the waterfalls. The following day, after crossing the border, travellers explore the [Argentine side near Puerto Iguazu](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/), where walkways bring them closer to the cascades and the Devil's Throat.

These walks call for comfortable shoes and a willingness to deal with humidity, spray and steps, but **they are not multi-day hikes**. Some programmes offer an optional boat ride near the falls; an available add-on must not be mistaken for an included service. On the Argentine side, the standard programme includes a flight to Buenos Aires after the park, so adding another long active outing that day would be difficult without changing the schedule.

The [classic 18-day tour through five countries](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/) spreads visits to the two sides of Iguazu across consecutive days. For travellers, the main attraction is experiencing different sections of the same natural wonder.

## Bolivia: the true off-road section

After stopping in northern Chile, travellers cross into Bolivia and board 4×4 vehicles. The route runs through Laguna Verde, the Salvador Dali Desert, the Polques hot springs and the Sol de Mañana geysers. It then continues to [Laguna Colorada](/bolivia/place/laguna-colorada/), a series of high-altitude lagoons and the [Uyuni Salt Flat](/bolivia/place/uyuni/).

The challenge here comes from **altitude, rough roads, cold nights and the remoteness of settlements**, rather than technical mountaineering. On the 18-day tour, the overnight stay on the desert plateau is described as basic, approaching expedition-style conditions. The journey then continues towards Uyuni and onward by air to La Paz.

The appearance of the Uyuni landscape depends on rainfall. Its mirror-like surface during the rainy season and the dry salt plain call for different driving conditions. Access to particular areas on the travel date and the length of the 4×4 day need to be checked against the current programme.

## Peru: mountain roads and archaeological routes

After La Paz, the journey proceeds via Tiwanaku and the Titicaca border area to Puno. Next come the road to [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/) and the excursion to [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/). Ascents, steps and walking at altitude can be tiring even without a dedicated sporting activity.

**In the standard programme, Machu Picchu is a one-day excursion involving a train, not a multi-day Inca Trail trek.** A genuine trekking itinerary would require a different programme and separate permits. Visitors to Machu Picchu follow designated circuits and timed entry slots, so the appropriate admission category is selected in advance.

In Peru, the adventure chiefly lies in changing natural conditions and travelling through the Andes amid cultural monuments. Rafting, mountain trekking or camping overnight cannot be promised automatically merely because the overall tour carries the "Adventure" theme.

## Which alternatives to compare

| Programme | Significant difference |
|---|---|
| 18 days, 5 countries | A closely scheduled Iguazu–Altiplano–Peru sequence |
| 19 days, 5 countries | Private format and Carnival in Rio |
| 20 days, 6 countries | Additional visit to Uruguay |
| 32 days, 8 countries | Extension into Ecuador and Colombia |

The [18-day group tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/) is useful for comparing the core off-road and cultural components. The [19-day private tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-carnival-private-tour/) adds Carnival, which affects travel dates but does not replace the high-altitude section. The [20-day journey](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) adds Uruguay. The [32-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/) continues into Ecuador and Colombia after Peru: a wider geographical range brings more travel stages, not necessarily more demanding sports.

{{catalog.tourTable:tour_source_5_stran_latinskoj_ameriki,tour_source_karnaval_5_stran,tour_latin_america_six_countries_20_days_2026,tour_south_america_eight_countries_32_days_2026}}

To compare other active options, browse [multi-country adventure tours](/multi-country/interests/adventure/) and [adventure trips in Bolivia](/interests/adventure/tours/bolivia/). When choosing, look at the actual number of 4×4 days, nights at altitude and included services.

## Altitude, clothing, borders and timing

The usual sequence takes travellers from humid Brazil through Argentina and Chile to high-altitude Bolivia, then Peru. The stop at [San Pedro de Atacama](/chile/place/san-pedro-de-atacama/) helps prepare for the ascent. Even in this order, altitude may affect how you feel: anyone with medical conditions or concerns should discuss the journey with a doctor in advance.

For Iguazu, lightweight quick-drying clothing and shoes with good grip are useful. On the Altiplano, pack warm layers and protection from sun and wind. When planning luggage, account for domestic flights, changes to overland transportation and the limited space for bags in a 4×4.

A journey involving these four countries cannot be planned as a string of neighbouring cities: international flights, the border crossing at Iguazu and the crossing between Chile and Bolivia all interact. Ada Tours helps coordinate the sequence, sensible connection times and documents according to travellers' nationality. Actual entry rules and access to natural attractions must be checked for the selected dates.

## Frequently asked questions about adventures in four countries

### Are mountaineering skills necessary?

There is no basis for treating them as a requirement for the standard programmes discussed here. The principal challenges are altitude, transfers and walks, not technical climbing.

### Where does the off-road driving take place?

In Bolivia, from the Chilean border through high-altitude lagoons to Uyuni. The confirmed format uses 4×4 vehicles; see the [18-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/) for details.

### Is hiking the Inca Trail included?

The standard programmes include an excursion to Machu Picchu using rail and other transport. A hiking itinerary requires a separate confirmed product and the relevant permits.

### Can I remove Chile and keep only the selected four countries?

In current tours, Chile connects the Argentine and Bolivian stages. The filter identifies shared principal countries but does not exclude others. Changing this logistics chain requires a separate itinerary.

## Four countries, four different cultural stories

**The cultural and historical appeal of this route lies in comparing several eras and traditions.** The Brazilian section introduces Rio de Janeiro, with its colonial buildings and modern urban setting. Argentina adds Buenos Aires, its neighbourhoods and tango. In Bolivia, the highlands connect with the archaeological site of Tiwanaku. Peru continues the story through Inca monuments in Cusco and Machu Picchu.

The Ada Tours catalogue includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}} covering all four countries and the culture-and-history theme. However, existing tours also travel through Chile, while longer options include Uruguay, Ecuador and Colombia. **The Argentina–Bolivia–Brazil–Peru filter identifies an intersection of principal countries within complete itineraries.** The programmes without a thematic filter can be found in the [catalogue for this country combination](/multi-country/argentina_bolivia_brazil_peru/).

## Brazil: Rio, from the historic centre to Corcovado

In [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/), the itinerary begins with the city's recognisable landmarks: Corcovado, Christ the Redeemer and Sugarloaf Mountain. An important cultural part of the visit, however, is in the older central districts. During the city tour, travellers see churches, monasteries, the cathedral and colonial-era buildings.

It helps to distinguish a panoramic sightseeing excursion from a historical walking route through the city. A hilltop view reveals the layout of Rio's bays, hills and neighbourhoods; exploring the centre tells a different story, that of a port and former capital. The [18-day five-country tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/) includes these experiences in its opening days before continuing to Iguazu.

Special Carnival versions also introduce samba culture. For example, the [Champions' Parade journey](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-rio-champions-parade-18-days/) centres on a specific event. **Carnival participation cannot automatically be promised on every tour through Brazil:** a special programme covering the relevant dates is needed.

## Argentina: Buenos Aires, tango and urban neighbourhoods

After seeing the Argentine side of Iguazu, travellers arrive in [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/). A city tour introduces Plaza de Mayo, historic neighbourhoods and well-known urban landmarks. The programmes also feature an evening tango show.

For visitors interested in history, the differences between neighbourhoods matter. Plaza de Mayo is connected to political history; San Telmo preserves older city buildings; La Boca reflects the port environment and a vivid visual culture; and Recoleta offers another perspective on architecture and urban life. Read the precise excursion itinerary before assuming a visit: listing the city does not guarantee free time in every neighbourhood.

**Tango is a cultural event here, not a sporting activity.** Some itineraries include it on an evening after the city tour. If your main aim is a dance workshop or visiting several milongas, that requires a different, more intensive programme to be arranged separately.

## Bolivia: Tiwanaku predates the Inca Empire

After the high-altitude natural landscapes of Bolivia, the route passes through La Paz and [Tiwanaku](/bolivia/place/tiwanaku/) towards the Peruvian border. Tiwanaku is an archaeological centre of an independent pre-Hispanic Andean civilisation. Its flourishing preceded the formation of the Inca Empire, so it would be misleading to regard the site as just another Inca city.

On the classic itinerary, travellers see the Gate of the Sun and the monumental remains of the ceremonial centre. The visit shows how Andean history was shaped by different cultural traditions across separate periods. At the next stage in Peru, the itinerary includes Lake Titicaca and the Uros Islands, with their reed constructions and local customs.

A visit to Tiwanaku is normally part of a long cross-border day. On the [18-day five-country tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/), the archaeological stop is followed by the drive to Puno. Time at the site depends on road conditions and border formalities; this is not a separate multi-day archaeological expedition in Bolivia.

## Peru: from Cusco to Machu Picchu

In [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/), itineraries combine Inca-period monuments with the architecture of the colonial city. Some confirmed programmes include Qorikancha, Sacsayhuaman, Qenqo, Puka Pukara and Tambomachay. Each site reveals a different part of the city's political and religious history, so check in advance which itinerary and how many stops are included in the particular excursion.

[Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/) continues the Inca theme, but it is a separate destination and a distinct excursion day. Its renowned stone structures, terraces and layout relate to life in the Inca state and the highland natural environment. The tour programmes discussed here arrange transport to the archaeological complex and a guided visit. **A multi-day trek along the Inca Trail is not automatically part of that arrangement.**

A Machu Picchu visit requires a selected official visitor circuit, date and time slot. If you want to see a particular part of the complex, the ticket purchase process and transportation must be arranged before travelling: you cannot arbitrarily exchange your booked route for another on arrival.

## Choosing a programme for an interest in history

| Itinerary | Cultural focus |
|---|---|
| 18 days, 5 countries | Rio, Buenos Aires, Tiwanaku, Cusco |
| 18 days with Carnival | Champions' Parade plus the cultural itinerary |
| 20 days, 6 countries | The same main centres plus Uruguay |
| 32 days, 8 countries | Extension beyond Peru into Ecuador and Colombia |

The [basic 18-day tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-group-tour-18-days/) traces a journey from Atlantic capitals and cities to ancient Andean monuments. The [18-day Carnival version](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-rio-champions-parade-18-days/) adds a specific Rio celebration to the cultural experience. The [20-day programme](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) includes Uruguay, while the [32-day itinerary](/multi-country/tour/south-america-eight-countries-32-days/) carries the story of the region beyond Peru into further countries.

## How much time to allow between sights

This itinerary involves several kinds of travel logistics. In Brazil and Argentina, flights and time for city tours are important. Between Bolivia and Peru, cultural stops are combined with an overland border crossing. Between Cusco and Machu Picchu, timing depends on transport schedules and the chosen entry slot.

The high altitude of the Andes affects even visitors who do not plan to trek: stone steps and long excursions require energy. On a busy itinerary, leave some quiet time after flying into a high-altitude city. Ada Tours helps coordinate the order of stops and excursion days, verify specific tickets and check document requirements in light of nationality and travel dates.

## Frequently asked questions about the four-country cultural route

### Did Tiwanaku and Machu Picchu belong to the same civilisation?

No. [Tiwanaku](/bolivia/place/tiwanaku/) is a centre of an earlier independent Andean culture, while [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/) is associated with the Inca Empire. Seeing both on one journey reveals the differences between these eras.

### Is tango included in the Argentine section?

Some itineraries include an evening tango show in Buenos Aires. Check the selected tour for the exact arrangements, tickets and format of the evening.

### Can I visit Machu Picchu without a multi-day hike?

Yes. Current programmes arrange transport and a guided visit to the complex; a multi-day hike on the Inca Trail is not necessary for that visit.

### Does every multi-country tour include Rio Carnival?

No. For Carnival, select a specially timed [Champions' Parade itinerary](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-5-countries-rio-champions-parade-18-days/) or another confirmed event-focused option. Standard Rio tours have a different cultural programme.

## From a celebration in Brazil to the monuments of the Andes

This selection brings together festive journeys that begin in [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/), travel through Argentina and Bolivia, and finish in Peru. The event takes place during the Brazilian stage: either Carnival celebrations, including the Champions' Parade on a dedicated itinerary, or New Year's Eve on Copacabana. The four countries named in the catalogue indicate countries visited on the tour, not four separate festivals.

The main difference from a short event-focused trip to Rio is the continuation through several cultural and natural regions. After [both sides of Iguazu](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/), travellers reach [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/) for city tours and tango; after high-altitude Bolivia, the Peruvian section begins with Lake Titicaca and Inca monuments.

Our selection includes {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. **Every programme actually visits five countries: Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Bolivia and Peru.** Chile cannot simply be dropped because it is absent from the selected four-country filter: it lies between the Argentine and Bolivian stages.

## What each of the four countries contributes

**Brazil: the date and occasion for the journey.** [Rio](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/) determines the calendar for the whole itinerary. Carnival with a visit to the Sambadrome and New Year's Eve on Copacabana are distinct options. After the celebration, the route continues to the [Brazilian side of Iguazu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/); the day spent in nature should be distinguished from the festival itself.

**Argentina: a transition from waterfalls to tango.** Around [Puerto Iguazu](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/), travellers can see the falls from Argentine trails and walkways. In Buenos Aires, the itinerary includes historic neighbourhoods and a tango show. This introduces the country's culture; it is not a promise of another Carnival event.

**Bolivia: the most demanding section for altitude and roads.** The journey through lagoons and the [Uyuni Salt Flat](/bolivia/place/uyuni/) is made by 4×4, then continues to [La Paz](/bolivia/place/la-paz/) and [Tiwanaku](/bolivia/place/tiwanaku/). Consider your energy, long transfers and general wellbeing in advance. Festival dates in Rio do not change the climate of this section.

**Peru: the historical climax.** After crossing the [Puno and Lake Titicaca area](/peru/place/puno-and-lake-titicaca/), the itinerary continues to [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/) and [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/), then Lima. For many travellers, this finale determines how much energy and how many days they should preserve after Carnival.

## Why Chile remains part of the route

Between Buenos Aires and Bolivia, current programmes include [Santiago de Chile](/chile/place/santiago-de-chile/), a flight to the Calama area and a stop in [San Pedro de Atacama](/chile/place/san-pedro-de-atacama/). The itinerary continues from there to Bolivia's lagoons. Chile is a full geographical stage of the journey, although no particular festival is included on the Chilean section of these tours.

If you specifically want only four countries without Chile, that requires different logistics and a different travel product. To compare the full range without the events filter, see the [Argentina–Bolivia–Brazil–Peru catalogue](/multi-country/argentina_bolivia_brazil_peru/).

For a comparison of festive options in the starting country, explore [events and festivals tours in Brazil](/interests/events-and-festivals/tours/brazil/); to focus on major cultural sights, browse [tours in Peru](/peru/tour/).

## Preparing for the journey from Rio to Machu Picchu

After a late festive evening, the journey continues with flights, excursions and road transfers. The sequence matters more than the number of named countries: Rio and Iguazu in the east, capitals and the Atacama, followed by the Bolivian highlands and the Peruvian Andes.

Different stages call for different clothing. Pack light clothes for humid Rio and warm layers for nights and early departures at altitude. Entry and transit requirements must be checked according to nationality and current rules in all five countries, including Chile, even if this page's filter displays four. We help coordinate logistics and preparation for each stage according to the chosen programme.

## Frequently asked questions about festive tours through Brazil, Argentina, Bolivia and Peru

### Can I combine Carnival and Machu Picchu?

Yes. Current programmes include a Carnival opening in Rio and a visit to Machu Picchu on the Peruvian stage. Check the specific event and the day of the ancient-city visit against the selected tour.

### Will there be a festival in Peru or Bolivia?

These itineraries are selected for an event in Brazil. Bolivia includes nature and historical stops; Peru includes Titicaca, Cusco and Machu Picchu. Separate local festivals in those countries are not confirmed as part of these programmes.

### Can I start the trip directly in Argentina?

In our festive itineraries, the event in Rio is the starting point for the travel calendar. Changing the starting country would require a tailored revision of the itinerary rather than simply removing the Brazilian days.

### What should I check before high-altitude excursions?

Consider your pace and health for long road transfers and time spent at altitude. Border-crossing requirements, insurance and the appropriate level of activity for each traveller should also be checked separately.

## What culinary experiences are actually included

**The main confirmed food experience on the current itinerary is a tango evening with dinner in Buenos Aires.** City tours, waterfalls, the salt flat and Inca monuments occupy most of the trip. Lunch is included on certain days, but a restaurant meal en route and a dedicated tasting experience are different things.

We offer {{catalog.toursCountPhrase}}. On the [20-day Six Countries of Latin America tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/), Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Peru are principal countries; Uruguay and Chile are also included. It is in Chile that an optional visit to the Maipo Valley wineries, with tasting, is offered. Chile is absent from this four-country filter's title but is part of the actual travel sequence. That distinction matters when choosing a programme under the "Food and Wine" theme.

| Stage | What is confirmed |
|---|---|
| Brazil | City sightseeing |
| Argentina | Tango show with dinner |
| Bolivia | Meals as specified by the itinerary |
| Peru | Lunches on excursion days |
| Chile | Winery visits at an additional cost |

## Argentina: dinner and tango, not a series of tastings

In [Buenos Aires](/argentina/place/buenos-aires/), one day combines a city excursion through [San Telmo](/argentina/place/san-telmo/), [La Boca](/argentina/place/la-boca/) and other neighbourhoods with an evening tango show. **Dinner is included with the show**, and the evening description mentions traditional dishes and Argentine wines. This is a meaningful combination of food and culture: travellers have a planned evening in a restaurant, not merely a suggestion to find dinner independently.

However, this itinerary does not contain a separate tour of Argentina's wineries, a cooking masterclass or a tasting circuit around Buenos Aires. If Argentine vineyards are your priority, look for a programme where they are named as independent excursions. The [Argentina food and wine catalogue](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/argentina/) helps compare appropriate trips by actual activities rather than a single culinary word in their descriptions.

The first part of the trip also includes [Brazilian Iguazu](/brazil/place/foz-do-iguacu/) and [Argentine Iguazu](/argentina/place/puerto-iguazu/). These days are devoted to the waterfalls and nature. They should not be considered culinary excursions simply because breakfast is on the schedule.

## Brazil: where there is time to discover local cuisine

The Brazilian section begins in [Rio de Janeiro](/brazil/place/rio-de-janeiro/) and continues to Iguazu. The itinerary includes a city tour, Corcovado, Sugarloaf Mountain and the flight to the falls. It does not list special cooking classes, organised food-market tastings or winery excursions on these days.

Travellers can therefore chiefly discover Brazilian cooking by choosing a restaurant independently, if there is enough free time. When comparing itineraries, check when an excursion ends and the next transfer begins: having a restaurant near the hotel does not automatically mean there is a free evening for dining.

In the [Brazil food and wine itinerary catalogue](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/brazil/), look for programmes where food is part of the sightseeing rather than simply a meal between excursions. This matters particularly on trips with a flight or early departure the next morning.

## Bolivia: high-altitude transfers determine meal arrangements

In Bolivia, the group travels by 4×4 through high-altitude lagoons, visits the [Uyuni](/bolivia/place/uyuni/) region and continues to [La Paz](/bolivia/place/la-paz/). The route includes an overnight stay in expedition-style accommodation, and some sections are above 4,000 metres. The programme here centres on natural attractions and logistics rather than restaurants.

Planned meals and lunches on the road should be understood as part of organising an expedition day. The inclusion of food does not imply a Bolivian cooking masterclass, a farm visit or a drinks tasting. If local cuisine is your main interest, allow separate time for it in a city, taking altitude and travel schedules into account.

After La Paz, the group heads to [Tiwanaku](/bolivia/place/tiwanaku/), then crosses the border into Peru. The day is busy with historical sights and transportation; the itinerary does not present it as free time for tastings.

## Peru: meals along the route and a dedicated culinary trip are different formats

The Peruvian section runs through [Puno and Lake Titicaca](/peru/place/puno-and-lake-titicaca/), [Cusco](/peru/place/cusco/), [Machu Picchu](/peru/place/machu-picchu/) and [Lima](/peru/place/lima/). Lunch is provided during the journey through the Andes and on the Machu Picchu day. These are confirmed meals, not a separate culinary tour of Peru's regions.

Exploring Peruvian gastronomy independently only makes sense where schedules and restaurant availability allow. For example, you could explore local dishes in Cusco and Lima outside excursion hours, but such a dinner cannot be described as an included service. Any additional restaurant plans are best assessed after looking at the whole day: excursions are scheduled in Cusco, followed by a flight to Lima.

If local food interests you more than the number of historical sights, compare this programme with [food and wine tours in Peru](/interests/food-and-wine/tours/peru/) and check whether tastings, farms and gastronomic excursions are named in the main programme rather than offered only as optional additions.

## Where the wine tasting fits into this journey

After Buenos Aires, the main itinerary passes through Chile, although the country is absent from the four-country page title. [Santiago de Chile](/chile/place/santiago-de-chile/) includes a city excursion. An additional visit to wineries in the [Maipo Valley](/chile/place/maipo-valley/), with wine tasting, is offered at extra cost and requires at least two participants.

This is the only winery excursion explicitly named in the itinerary. Its availability adds a more noticeable culinary element, but **does not turn the Argentina–Bolivia–Brazil–Peru selection into a standalone wine tour of those four countries**. If tasting wine is essential to your journey, confirm the excursion's status and feasibility before committing to the overall route.

## Who this option suits

Choose the [20-day tour](/multi-country/tour/latin-america-6-countries-20-days/) if your main aim is to see Rio, Iguazu, Buenos Aires, the Andes and Peru's monuments, with the tango dinner and possible wine tasting in Chile as pleasant additions. A trip structured around restaurants, wineries and cooking experiences throughout would need a different itinerary.

The composition of the countries and transfers is explained on the [general Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil and Peru page](/multi-country/argentina_bolivia_brazil_peru/). The criterion here is different: count only a specifically confirmed activity as a culinary experience, rather than every included meal.
